rationale:
Quota is 1 long, 3 Shorts and 0 carousels. The playbook says to ship broad searched questions only and to follow the long-form queue. Queue #1, Nausea Foods, was re-rendered on 11-17. Months 2–6 is live. So today's long video is queue #2, Mounjaro vs Zepbound. The verified 11-16 script was held for beat drift, so this is a fixed re-render, not a new angle. It is a search-demand format with steady high search (radar momentum 84), and it rests fully on the two US PIs, which keeps fact-check risk low. Today's breaking news goes into Shorts or nowhere: NAION is peaking but already had a Short on 11-10, and the teens trial is a caution topic that isn't a felt moment.

The Shorts follow the slot rules:
- **S1, 08:00:** a visible pen moment ('my pen looks different') that is also the required spin-off of L1's device chapter. It sends viewers to the Pen how-to.
- **S2, 13:00:** a practical eating moment (fibre when you're barely hungry). This week's small UK study is only a one-line hedged hook, never the topic.
- **S3, 20:00:** the holiday-table drinks moment, targeting Thanksgiving.

All 3 Shorts are felt or practical moments. Each one avoids angles used in the last 30 days: pen storage, flying, clicks, liquid check, injection-site reactions, full after 3 bites, holiday heartburn, and the low-blood-sugar-with-alcohol angle are all excluded.

Mix: emerging or rising (S2, S3), evergreen with a timely hook (L1), and a gentle myth correction (S1: a different-looking pen isn't a different or stronger medicine). Pillars rotate (is-it-for-you, life-on-glp1 ×2, get-the-most). Body systems vary: device, gut and hydration.

Skipped: the teens trial (caution, and parents' questions need a full long with a same-day approval check), the brain review (caution, not a felt moment), and all cost, pharmacy and surgery topics (banned).

pieces.topic: Mounjaro vs Zepbound: same medicine (tirzepatide), different US-approved uses, labels and device options. Fixed re-render of the verified, held 11-16 script (playbook queue #2)
pieces.angle:
Re-render and resubmit the verified 11-16 script. Fix its known faults first:
- Rebuild every cut from the final word timestamps (the render had 76% on time; the target is every cut within 0.5 s of its beat).
- Cut the description from about 1,340 characters to a tight plain-text one that ends '…whether it's right for you.'
- Remove the #Type2Diabetes and #WeightManagement hashtags.
- Every minus figure is spoken as 'loss' or 'lower'.

Content stays locked:
- Sentence 1 names tirzepatide and the title's question. By 15 s, the short answer: both US labels list the same active ingredient, tirzepatide. The difference is the approved uses.
- Second payoff at 15–30 s: each PI's Section 1 indication, quoted word for word with its population. Mounjaro (PI rev. 27 Aug 2026): type 2 diabetes, including the paediatric indication as printed. Zepbound (PI rev. 28 Aug 2026): chronic weight management and OSA, as printed.
- The trial programme behind each label (SURPASS, SURMOUNT, SURMOUNT-OSA), each with its full population.
- 'Different trial populations, so the side-effect tables can't be compared head to head.'
- Devices: only those printed in each PI's How Supplied section, each IFU at its own verified URL. No amounts.
- One GI line: 'mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time'.
- No cost, insurance, dosing or switching talk. No standalone 'Picture this' scene after the answer.
- Required lines: the don't-switch/stop/change line, 'Not personal advice', the full prescriber line, and the ending 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.'

Publisher: put a '▶ Watch next' link to How It Works after the first paragraph, and add the video to 'Life on Tirzepatide'.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide: Mounjaro vs Zepbound, What's Different?
pieces.why: Queue #2 in the playbook. A search-demand head-to-head format (approved labels only) with steady high search, built entirely on primary labels so it can pass the fact-check today. Fewer than 2 of the last 7 long videos that shipped were search-demand formats.

pieces.topic: Your tirzepatide pen looks different from someone else's: single-dose pen vs KwikPen vs vial, and why a different device doesn't mean a different medicine
pieces.angle: Sentence 1 as written. Then: the US tirzepatide labels list more than one device, naming only those printed in each PI's How Supplied section. Add 'In Australia, Mounjaro comes as a KwikPen' (verified via the TGA/medsinfo consumer leaflet). Add the UK only if the UK SmPC or patient leaflet confirms it. Myth line: 'A different device doesn't mean a different medicine: the active ingredient is tirzepatide in each. Your dose is set by your prescriber, and it can differ from someone else's.' No mention of doses, clicks, strengths, leftover medicine or getting extra doses from a pen. Then: each device has its own steps, so follow the leaflet in your box and ask a pharmacist to show you. 'Don't swap devices on your own.' Then 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and the loop line. Cite each IFU at its own URL.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide Pen Looks Different From Yours? #shorts
pieces.target_keyword: mounjaro kwikpen vs single dose pen
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1 and a visible pen moment, the proven 08:00 winner (pen blood 111 here and 637 on TikTok). It also serves UK/AU viewers whose packs differ. | fact-check: A good reassurance topic, but there's a real safety edge. The KwikPen is a multi-dose pen and the others are single-dose, so device talk can slide into dose, click or extra-dose talk, which is self-titration territory. Checked: in Australia, Mounjaro comes as a KwikPen (the TGA-listed 'Mounjaro KwikPen' consumer leaflet lists tirzepatide as the active ingredient). The UK KwikPen still has to be checked against the UK SmPC or patient leaflet, or dropped. For the US, don't promise in advance that three devices are listed: name only what each PI's How Supplied section prints. The myth line also needs care. A different device isn't a different medicine, but a friend's dose may well be different from yours. Don't let 'not stronger' suggest that every pen holds the same dose.

pieces.topic: Barely hungry on tirzepatide: making a small plate still bring fibre, without making the stomach worse
pieces.angle: Sentence 1 as written. Label fact on its own: tirzepatide reduces appetite and food intake (label wording). Optional hook, only if verified: 'A UK review found little research on diet quality during these medicines. One study it covered reported low fibre intake. That's early evidence, not proof.' Otherwise skip the hook and go straight to habits. Advisory habits at their exact wording: build fibre up gradually and pair it with fluids, unless you've been told to limit fluids. Untagged idea: add one fibre food you already like to the small plate you eat (beans, berries, oats, vegetables). Suggest asking about a dietitian. No grams, calories, supplements or 'bad' foods. Then 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and the loop line.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide: Eating Less, Getting Enough Fibre? #shorts
pieces.why: A fresh practical-moment angle on our second-best long-form topic (What to Eat). It uses this week's nutrition coverage only as evidence, never as the topic, and keeps the 13:00 slot off news. | fact-check: A useful, safe angle that stays clear of restrictive eating. I couldn't find the 'small UK study of 14 people on GLP-1 medicines'. The closest verifiable UK source is a Cambridge/UCL review in Obesity Reviews. It found only 12 studies on diet alongside semaglutide or tirzepatide, and reported fibre intake about half the recommended amount in one study. Don't use an unverified n=14 study as the hook. Either find the primary paper and confirm its sample, design and finding, or use the review with a hedge, or drop the study line. Quote the 2025 joint advisory word for word, and keep its 'first few days' nausea note at that exact scope. Don't attach the label's appetite wording to fibre advice. No grams target, because a number can read as a nutrition prescription. Keep 'unless you've been told to limit fluids' word for word. Add 'If fibre makes your stomach worse, tell your prescriber.'

pieces.topic: Holiday party drinks on tirzepatide: why a fuller, slower stomach and GI side effects make pacing and fluids matter
pieces.angle: Reframe the topic as: 'Holiday drinks on tirzepatide: what the label covers, and simple pacing habits to ask your prescriber about.' Sentence 1 as written. By 6 s: 'The label doesn't specifically address alcohol' (only if confirmed). Then separate label sentences: it delays gastric emptying. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea are common. Fluid loss from them has been linked to kidney problems (label wording). No 'so' or 'that's why' between them. Caveat clause: low blood sugar risk is higher for people with diabetes on insulin or a sulfonylurea. Untagged tips: sip water alongside, unless you've been told to limit fluids. Eat something with protein. Skipping the drink is fine too. We can't give a safe amount, so ask your prescriber. Emergency card: 'If you have severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting, stop using it and call your healthcare provider right away.' Then: 'For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.' Then 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and the loop line. No craving research, no dates.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide at a Holiday Party: What About Drinks? #shorts
pieces.why: The playbook's 20:00 holiday-table slot runs 11-18 to 11-27 and lists drinks at a party. Party-season searches are rising, and this angle (stomach and fluids) differs from the 11-12 low-blood-sugar Short. | fact-check: The topic line says 'why a fuller, slower stomach and GI side effects make pacing and fluids matter'. That links gastric emptying to an outcome as cause and effect, which the craft rules ban and the label doesn't support. Drop the 'why'. Alcohol content also carries risks: it reads as a 'safe amount' if hedged badly, and the pancreatitis and low blood sugar framing must stay at label scope. The angle mostly handles this. Keep these conditions. (1) Say the label doesn't specifically address alcohol only after checking the current Zepbound and Mounjaro PIs (28 and 27 Aug 2026) and confirming it. (2) Each label fact gets its own sentence, with no causal link between them. (3) Low blood sugar only for people with diabetes on insulin or a sulfonylurea, stated in the spoken line. (4) Never suggest drinking is expected. Add a no-pressure line such as 'Skipping the drink is always fine too.' (5) Holiday framing is fine for a timed Short, but keep 'this year' and dates out of the narration and on-screen text. The emergency line and the scoped don't-stop line must be copied exactly.
